title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Introduction
Deciding whether and how to tell a partner about an HIV diagnosis is one of the hardest steps for many people living with HIV. Disclosure can bring support and protect a partner’s health, but it can also lead to stigma, rejection, or violence. PHIA surveys across sub-Saharan Africa show that many people living with HIV have not shared their status, and fear of stigma and relationship conflict are common reasons.
This artifact is a working AI assistant that I designed, built, and tested to support these decisions without pushing users in either direction.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Description
The assistant works in three modes, chosen by the user at the start:

(A) Personal support for someone considering disclosing their own status.
(B) Supporter mode for someone helping another person.
(C) Research mode for students and researchers, answering only from uploaded PHIA summary sheets, with citations and evidence levels.

In personal modes, it always checks safety first, asks one question at a time, describes options neutrally (including waiting and provider-assisted partner notification), and shares verified support services for Uganda and Zimbabwe. It never gives medical or legal advice, never tells anyone whether to disclose, and never invents statistics or contact details.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Objective
To show how a generative AI tool can be designed for a sensitive public health topic so that it is safe, private, neutral, and grounded in verified evidence, and to identify the specific safeguards such a tool needs before it could be used by an HIV program.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Process
I followed the five stages of Design Thinking:

Empathize. I started from what my PHIA research shows about why people do not disclose, and from the risks disclosure can carry.
Define. Before building, I tested three existing AI tools (a general LLM, a published HIV-support GPT, and the STORM research assistant). I found recurring problems: wording that subtly favored disclosure, uncritical acceptance of user claims, drift away from the intended audience, and unverifiable citations.
Ideate. I turned each problem into a design rule, such as a fixed safety check, user modes chosen at the start, and answers limited to verified sources.
Prototype. I built the assistant in Chatbase, uploading six PHIA summary sheets and a support resource list for Uganda and Zimbabwe that I checked against recent sources.
Test and iterate. I ran two rounds of scenario tests, revised the instructions after the first round, and confirmed the fixes in the second.


Test results

  13 / 13scenario tests passed across two rounds
  4issues found in Round 1 and fixed in Round 2
  0invented statistics or contact details

Tools and Technologies Used

Chatbase: no-code platform used to build, train, and publish the assistant from uploaded documents.
PHIA summary sheets: Uganda (UPHIA 2020–2021), Zimbabwe (ZIMPHIA 2020), Malawi, Lesotho, Eswatini, and Mozambique.
Verified support resource list: GBV, HIV, and legal aid services for Uganda and Zimbabwe.

title: HIV Disclosure Support Assistant
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
This assistant offers HIV programs a tested model for AI-supported disclosure counseling: it puts safety first, stays neutral about disclosure, and answers only from verified PHIA data and checked local resources. It passed all 13 safety, privacy, neutrality, and accuracy tests, and every PHIA figure it reported matched the original source. Unlike general chatbots I tested, it does not accept unverified claims or invent statistics.


Relevance
Global health organizations are under pressure to use AI, but in stigmatized areas like HIV, a careless tool can push people toward unsafe disclosure or spread false information. This artifact gives program managers and researchers a practical checklist of safeguards to require before deploying a health chatbot, along with a working example. It also shows that any real deployment would first need to address data protection, since the platform’s terms do not cover health data.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
text:
AI is often described as objective. But every model starts with human decisions: which data to collect, which outcome to predict, and which measure to use when the thing we care about is hard to observe. When those choices are careless, an algorithm can quietly reproduce existing inequities at scale.
In this paper, I use a landmark case of algorithmic bias in health care to examine where bias comes from, and I set out the leadership practices I will use to prevent it in public health research, including my own work with HIV survey data.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
section: How Bias Entered a Health Algorithm
text:
How Bias Entered a Health Algorithm
In 2019, Obermeyer and colleagues showed in Science that a widely used tool for identifying patients who needed extra care had a hidden flaw. It used past healthcare spending as a stand-in for health need. Because less money had historically been spent on Black patients with the same level of illness, the algorithm judged them to be healthier than they were.

  1 · Human choiceUse healthcare spending as a proxy for health need
  2 · Historical gapLess was spent on Black patients with the same illness level
  3 · Model learnsLower spending is read as "healthier"
  4 · HarmPatients who needed extra care were overlooked

No one intended to discriminate. The bias entered at step 1, through a convenient measure, and the model faithfully carried it forward.
Where a leader can intervene:

  Before building: question whether the proxy measures what matters
  During evaluation: check results across subgroups, not only overall accuracy
  After deployment: keep human judgment and invite people to raise concerns

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
text:
The Paper






NoteNavigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective



In 2019, Obermeyer and colleagues published a study in Science that showed how bias can enter healthcare algorithms. They looked at a widely used tool that helped hospitals identify patients who needed extra care. The algorithm used past healthcare spending as a stand-in for health need. Because less money has historically been spent on Black patients with the same level of illness, the algorithm treated them as healthier than they were. Many patients who needed support were overlooked.
What stands out to me is that no one intended to discriminate. The bias came from a human choice: using a convenient measure instead of a more accurate one. This example shows that AI does not remove human bias. It can carry forward the choices people make when they select data, define outcomes, or choose proxy variables.

Personal Value Statement
I believe that data and AI tools used in public health should help identify real needs and disparities, not hide them. As someone who has worked with large-scale HIV survey data across multiple countries, I have seen how decisions about what to measure and how to define key variables can shape what the results appear to show. As a leader in health data science, my responsibility is to question these choices early and to keep fairness and transparency in mind throughout the research process. I value careful thinking, clear documentation of limitations, and the willingness to revise methods when they may produce skewed results.


Strategies to Fulfill This
Question Proxy Variables and Outcome Definitions. Before building or adopting a model, ask whether the variables truly measure what matters (for example, using healthcare spending or clinic visits as proxies for health need). Involve people with different perspectives, such as clinicians, community partners, and researchers, when defining outcomes, especially in areas such as HIV care engagement or treatment adherence.
Check Results Across Groups. Regularly examine model performance and findings by key subgroups (race/ethnicity, gender, age, geography, or socioeconomic status). Treat this as an ongoing practice rather than a final step. Document who is underrepresented in the data and how that may affect conclusions.
Document Assumptions and Limitations. Clearly state the assumptions behind variable selection and modeling choices in reports and presentations. Make it standard practice to discuss potential sources of bias, rather than only reporting overall accuracy.
Keep Human Judgment in the Process. Use AI or statistical models as tools to support decisions, not as final answers. Encourage team members to question results that seem inconsistent with known patterns in the population, and create space for them to raise concerns.
Build Diverse Review Practices. Include people from different backgrounds and roles when reviewing study design, variable choices, and model outputs. Different perspectives can help identify blind spots that a more uniform team might miss.
Lead Change Openly. When introducing new AI tools or methods to a team, start with small pilots and share both successes and problems openly. Explain why changes are being made, invite questions and pushback, and treat concerns about bias as useful input rather than resistance.


Conclusion
AI and data science tools reflect the decisions people make when collecting data, choosing measures, and interpreting results. Strong leadership in public health research means making these decisions more intentionally, with a clear focus on equity and the real needs of the populations being studied. It also means guiding teams through change in a transparent and inclusive way.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
text:
Description
The paper has three parts:

A case analysis of the Obermeyer et al. (2019) study, showing how a proxy variable turned historical inequity into an algorithmic decision.
A personal value statement grounded in my experience with multi-country HIV survey data.
Six leadership strategies that turn that value into everyday practice, from questioning proxy variables to leading change openly.


  1landmark study of algorithmic bias, published in Science
  6leadership strategies for fair, transparent health AI
  3data-challenge scenarios where I applied these ideas


Applying these ideas in practice
In a separate AIML-500 simulation (Activity 4.3), I worked through three realistic data challenges with an AI coach. In the résumé-screening scenario, I identified proxy discrimination and selective labels, the same mechanism behind the Obermeyer case, and proposed local validation, subgroup fairness checks, staged deployment, human oversight, and rollback thresholds. In the hospital data-sharing scenario, I proposed federated learning with data harmonization and governance, while recognizing that privacy techniques reduce risk but do not remove it. The simulation showed me that the strategies in this paper can be turned into concrete decisions about real data.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective

Objective
To show how human choices introduce bias into AI systems, using a well-documented health care example, and to define the concrete leadership practices I will use to keep public health data and AI tools fair, transparent, and focused on real needs.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
text:
Process

Studied a well-documented case. I chose the Obermeyer et al. (2019) study because it shows bias entering through an ordinary design choice rather than bad intent.
Traced the mechanism. I identified the exact point where bias entered: using spending as a proxy for need.
Connected it to my own work. I reflected on how variable definitions in HIV survey research shape what results appear to show.
Wrote a personal value statement and strategies. I turned that value into six practices a team can actually follow.
Used AI for language only. I used Claude to refine language and improve clarity, then reviewed and edited the final content myself.
Adapted it for this portfolio. I added the visual of how bias moved through the algorithm, the three points where a leader can intervene, and evidence from the Activity 4.3 simulation showing how I applied these ideas.

title: Navigating Human Bias in Public Health AI: A Leader’s Perspective
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
I combine hands-on experience with population health data and an understanding of how AI systems fail. I can spot where a convenient measure may hide a disparity, explain it clearly to a team, and put practical checks in place, such as subgroup analysis, documented assumptions, and human review, before a model shapes real decisions.


Relevance
Public health programs are adopting AI to decide who receives outreach, testing, or care. If those tools use biased proxies, the people with the greatest need can be the first to be missed. Leaders who question these choices early help programs use AI to reveal disparities rather than hide them. This is the role I want to play in global health.

title: Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?
text:
Introduction
New AI health products often arrive with impressive numbers: a low monthly price, a fast treatment plan, a high model score. For a health program, the hard part is knowing what those numbers do and do not show before trusting the tool with patients.
This artifact comes from From Insight to Action, a nine-page newsletter my AIML-500 group wrote about three AI products launched in October 2026, in food service, logistics, and healthcare. I researched and wrote the healthcare case study: Nolla Health’s AI-assisted acne care pilot in Utah.

title: Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?
text:
Description
The newsletter explains what each product does, how it could change business decisions, and what evidence is still missing. My healthcare section covers:

What’s new: Nolla Derm’s Utah acne-prescription pilot (October 5, 2026) and its AI flare-up forecasting feature (October 9, 2026).
How it works: identity check, medical questions, a five-angle face scan, AI review, and, in the pilot’s first stage, approval of each prescription by two physicians.
Commercial impact: faster, cheaper access for patients and possibly more doctor time for difficult cases, set against the lack of independent clinical evidence.
Limitations: skin-tone differences, missed diagnoses, privacy, side effects, and who is responsible if something goes wrong.


  3industries compared: food, logistics, healthcare
  8cited sources, including a state regulator and The BMJ
  10dropped-text errors found and fixed for this portfolio version


Reading the claims carefully
The core of my section is separating what the company reports from what has actually been shown:







Company claim
What the evidence actually shows




Flare-up model AUROC of 0.900
AUROC measures how well a model ranks higher-risk above lower-risk cases. It does not mean the model is 90% accurate for every patient, and the result comes from an internal, retrospective evaluation, not an independent clinical trial.


Plans from $4.99 per month; a treatment plan in about 10–15 minutes
Advertised by the company. These figures say nothing about whether outcomes match a visit with a dermatologist.


“AI prescriptions”
A limited Utah pilot: certain adults, mild-to-moderate acne, a small set of topical treatments, and two physicians approving each prescription in stage one. It is not autonomous prescribing.









Product overview: what’s new and how the pilot works.







Business analysis: AUROC explained, commercial impact, and limitations.







What this means for global health
The questions I asked about Nolla are the same ones an HIV or global health program should ask before adopting any AI tool. Was the model tested independently, or only by the company? Does a high score hold across the populations the program serves, including people with darker skin tones? Who reviews the AI’s output, and who is accountable when it is wrong? A tool that performs well in one setting may not transfer to clinics in sub-Saharan Africa without local validation.

title: Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?
text:
Objective
To analyze a real, newly launched AI product in healthcare and explain its business value and its risks in plain language for a business audience, while reading model performance metrics correctly instead of repeating company claims.

title: Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?
text:
Process

Chose the case within the assignment window. Our group was asked to cover AI products launched within one month. The Nolla pilot started two days before the window, so we included it because the October 9 flare-up forecasting feature fell inside it, and we stated this openly in the newsletter.
Gathered evidence from different types of sources. I used Nolla’s own announcements for product facts, the Utah Department of Commerce for the pilot’s authorized scope and oversight, and The BMJ for independent reporting on physician oversight.
Interpreted the model metrics. I explained AUROC for non-technical readers and labeled the 0.900 and 0.914 results as internal, retrospective evaluations.
Mapped the human oversight. I summarized the patient pathway (intake, face scan and AI review, two-physician approval, prescription) to show where people stay in control.
Integrated with the group. Our group combined the three case studies into one newsletter with a shared structure and a cross-industry comparison of how much human review each use of AI needs.
Revised for this portfolio. I found that the PDF export had silently dropped emphasized text in ten places. In my section, one sentence’s meaning was reversed: it read that an AUROC of 0.900 “does mean” 90% accuracy. I restored the missing text across the newsletter and corrected that sentence.

Tools and Technologies Used

Primary sources: Nolla Health announcements, the Utah Department of Commerce AI pilot program, and The BMJ.
ML evaluation concepts: AUROC and the difference between internal retrospective testing and independent prospective trials.
Generative AI: used by our group to support research synthesis and the newsletter’s HTML design, as disclosed in the newsletter.

title: Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
I can look past the headline numbers of an AI health product and explain what they really mean. In this case study I showed that a high AUROC is not the same as accuracy, that a company’s internal test is not a clinical trial, and that “AI prescribing” was in practice a narrow pilot with two doctors approving every prescription. I explain this in language that business and program decision-makers can follow.


Relevance
Health programs are approached by vendors with AI tools and promising metrics. Being able to ask the right questions about validation, fairness across populations, human oversight, and accountability helps programs avoid tools that look strong on paper but have not been proven for the people they serve. This connects directly to my goal of helping global health programs adopt AI that is evidence-based and safe.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Introduction
Global health programs are under pressure to “use AI,” and deep learning often gets the most attention. But a more complex model is not always a better one. Choosing the wrong approach can waste limited budgets, need data a program does not have, or produce results that staff cannot explain.
In this report, I compare two real-world cases to show how the type of data should guide the choice between traditional machine learning and deep learning.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Description
The report analyzes two examples from my AIML-500 coursework, each linked to a real-world application:

Machine learning: Customer churn prediction at a telecom company, using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) on structured customer records. A 2022 PLOS ONE study reached about 99% accuracy with only 3,333 customers.
Deep learning: Apple’s Face ID, which uses Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on over a billion images to recognize faces from raw pixels.

For each case, I explain why the chosen approach fits the problem and why the other approach does not, then compare both side by side.

  2real-world cases analyzed
  6factors compared: data type, features, data size, computing, explainability, priority
  4cited sources, including a peer-reviewed study









Factor
Churn prediction (ML, SVM)
Facial recognition (DL, CNN)




Data type
Structured table
Unstructured images (raw pixels)


Feature extraction
Chosen by people
Learned automatically


Data size
Small to moderate
Very large


Computing power
Ordinary computer
Specialized hardware


Explainability
High
Low


Main priority
Fast, low-cost, explainable predictions
High accuracy and security




What this means for global health
The same reasoning applies to my own field. Much of the data HIV programs work with, such as PHIA survey records, is structured: one row per respondent with clearly defined variables. Like churn data, this kind of data is usually a better fit for traditional machine learning, which works with moderate sample sizes and keeps results explainable to program staff. Deep learning becomes the better choice when the data is raw and unstructured, such as medical images, and large labeled datasets and computing resources are available.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Objective
To learn how to tell the difference between machine learning and deep learning, and to practice justifying a technical choice with real data and credible sources, a skill I need to advise health programs on which AI tools actually fit their problems.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Process

Reviewed the lesson. I studied the course’s ML and DL examples and the three key differences: feature extraction, data requirements, and model complexity.
Selected and researched two cases. I chose one example of each approach and found real-world evidence: a peer-reviewed churn study in PLOS ONE and Apple’s official Face ID security documentation.
Built the argument. For each case, I explained why the chosen approach fits and why the opposite approach does not, using four questions: What type of data is it? How much data is there? Do the results need to be explained? What does it cost?
Revised against the rubric. I checked that every claim was supported by a source, made numbers consistent throughout, removed one claim my sources did not support, and formatted citations in APA style.
Adapted it for this portfolio. I added the global health section above to show how the same decision framework applies to HIV survey data.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Tools and Technologies Used

AIML-500 lesson materials: ML vs. DL examples and key differences.
Research sources: PLOS ONE (peer-reviewed journal), Apple Platform Security Guide, AIMultiple.
Microsoft Word and APA 7 citation style: writing and formatting the report.
Quarto and GitHub Pages: publishing this portfolio page.

title: Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach
text:
Value Proposition

Unique Value
I can explain technical AI choices in plain language and back them with evidence. This report shows that I can look at a problem, identify what kind of data it involves, and explain clearly why one approach fits better than another, in a way that non-technical decision-makers can follow.


Relevance
Health programs often have limited budgets and small or structured datasets. Knowing when a simpler, explainable machine learning model is enough, and when deep learning is truly needed, helps programs avoid costly tools that do not fit their data. This connects directly to my goal of helping global health programs adopt AI that is evidence-based and appropriate for the people they serve.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
Personal Value Proposition

As an HIV epidemiology researcher building skills in AI and machine learning, I help global health programs adopt AI tools that are grounded in population-based evidence such as PHIA data. I design and test these tools for the safety, privacy, and neutrality that sensitive health topics require, so that they support the people they serve rather than put them at risk.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
About Me
I am an HIV epidemiology researcher. My work uses data from the Population-based HIV Impact Assessment (PHIA) surveys in Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, and Zimbabwe to study HIV status non-disclosure: who does not share their HIV status, and why.
I am currently studying machine learning fundamentals in the AIML-500 course at Indiana Wesleyan University. My goal is to connect these two fields: to help HIV and global health programs use AI in ways that are evidence-based, respect privacy, and protect people in stigmatized situations.

title: Yuchen Gu
text:
Artifacts
Each artifact below is a finished piece of work from my AIML-500 coursework, with the process, tools, and value it offers to global health programs.

Artifact 1 · Chatbot

HIV Disclosure Support Assistant

Artifact 2 · Case Study Report

Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning: Choosing the Right Approach

Artifact 3 · Newsletter Case Study (Group)

Can AI Help with Acne Care Without Losing Human Oversight?

How a convenient proxy variable carried racial bias into a widely used health algorithm, and six leadership practices I use to keep public health data and AI tools fair and transparent.
